traveler: Alfonso X el Sabio, king of Castile and Leon
title: The King Who Had It Written Down: Alfonso X, the Scriptorium, the Frontier, and the Son
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Toledo, born on the feast of San Clemente
stops.date_confidence: attested: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_de_Castilla gives 23 November 1221 at Toledo. No contemporary source names the palace or the room; the coordinate is the old-city landmark, not a confirmed birth site.
stops.campa: A son is born to Fernando III of Castile and to Beatriz of Suabia, granddaughter of an emperor. The city is not a century back in Christian hands and still runs on three tongues at once: Arabic in the markets and in the manuals, Hebrew in the study houses, Castilian in the chancery that is only beginning to be a chancery. The child inherits two claims in the same hour, his father's kingdom and, through his mother, a line running back into the Hohenstaufen. No document of the time names the house or the room. The record keeps the day and the parents and stops there.
suggested_refs: The Toledo of the three languages, seedbed of the translation workshops he will later run as royal business

stops.name: Burgos, sworn to as heir
stops.date_confidence: attested: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_de_Castilla dates the Burgos assembly to 21 March 1222.
stops.campa: Four months past his first birthday the infante is carried into an assembly at Burgos and the magnates of Castile swear to him as heir. He cannot walk the length of the hall and cannot follow a word of the oath. The kingdom they are promising him does not yet include Leon, which his father will inherit eight years later, nor Seville, nor Murcia, nor Niebla, nor Cadiz. Almost everything the oath will one day cover has still to be taken, and the armies that take it are the ones this child grows up inside. He is fourteen months old on the day of the swearing.
suggested_refs: The Castilian cortes and the practice of swearing to an infant heir

stops.name: Jerez de la Frontera, the raid fought in his name
stops.date_confidence: campaign and year attested [A]; any personal role for Alfonso is [R] and is contradicted by the source itself, which gives command to Alvar Perez de Castro. Alfonso was nine. Month and day not fixed.
stops.campa: A Castilian column goes down into lower Andalusia in the infante's name: Salamanca, Toledo, Andujar, Cordoba, Palma del Rio, and a battle near Jerez. It is the first campaign carried under his name and he directs no part of it: Alfonso is nine years old. Fernando III orders Alvar Perez de Castro to ride with him, to guard the boy and to command the host, because the infante is too young and not yet hardened and Alvar Perez is. The chronicle written under Alfonso decades later remembers this raid as the blow from which the Muslims of Andalusia never recovered.
stops.quote: Mandó a don Alvar de Castro, el Castellano, que fuese con él, para guardar el infante y por cabdillo de la hueste, ca el infante era muy moço e avn non era tan esfforçado, e don Alvar Pérez era omne deferido e muy esforçado.
stops.quote_source: Royal chronicle material on the 1231 lower-Andalusia cabalgada, quoted in es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_de_Castilla citing Martinez Diez, Alfonso X el Sabio (2000), p. 306
suggested_refs: Gonzalo Martinez Diez, Alfonso X el Sabio (2000), pp. 306, 634-635, for the 1231 cabalgada and its chronicle memory

stops.name: Toro, the death of his mother
stops.date_confidence: attested: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatriz_de_Suabia gives 5 November 1235 at Toro. An earlier pool entry placed the death at Toledo; that is wrong and is corrected here.
stops.campa: Beatriz of Suabia dies at Toro on the fifth of November. Alfonso is thirteen. She is carried north and buried at Santa Maria la Real de Las Huelgas in Burgos, among the Castilian royal dead, and there she lies for forty-four years. In 1279 he has her bones lifted out of that abbey and brought south to Seville, to lie beside his father in the city the two of them took together. He has been king twenty-seven years by then and has five years left to live.
suggested_refs: Santa Maria la Real de Las Huelgas, Burgos, her first grave, 1235-1279

stops.name: Burgos, a son born outside any marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the child and the mother by es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Fernandez_el_Nino; the sources divide between c. 1240 and 1242 for the birth. The place is a placement only: the record says Castile and the court was itinerant, so Burgos stands here for the court and is not an attestation.
stops.campa: Before any marriage has been arranged for him the infante fathers a son on Elvira Rodriguez de Villada. The boy is called Alfonso Fernandez and will be known all his life as el Nino, the child. He will marry Blanca Alfonso de Molina and hold Molina and Mesa in her right, and he will die in 1281, three years before his father. Of the mother the record keeps a name and nothing more. Alfonso is eighteen or nineteen. The year itself is argued: some sources say 1240, some 1242.
suggested_refs: Alfonso Fernandez el Nino, lord consort of Molina and Mesa, d. 1281

stops.name: Alcaraz, the treaty that buys a kingdom
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1243 and for the place: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tratado_de_Alcaraz sites the treaty at Alcaraz in Albacete, not at Murcia. Month and day not fixed in the sources reached here.
stops.campa: At Alcaraz in the uplands of Albacete the Hudi lords of Murcia hand their emirate to Castile on terms: the ruling house keeps its place, Muslims keep their property, their law and their worship, Castile takes the fortresses and the revenue. The infante is twenty-one and this is his negotiation. What is signed in the hills is not a conquest but a protectorate, and it will hold twenty-one years before it breaks in his hands. Lorca and Mula hold out into the spring of 1244, Cartagena until early 1245.
suggested_refs: The Treaty of Alcaraz, 1243, and the legal status of the Mudejar communities it created

stops.name: Murcia, entering the Alcazar Mayor
stops.date_confidence: attested for the campaign of 1243-1245; the month is an ordering device, not a record. The Alcazar Mayor is gone under later convent and cathedral building and the coordinate is approximate to the historic precinct.
stops.campa: He rides into Murcia and takes the Alcazar Mayor, the seat the treaty has delivered, while the Hudi emir keeps his title and loses the keys. It is the richest thing Castile has ever acquired without a siege. He will come back to this city as king, will lose it to revolt in 1264, will receive it back from another king's army, and at the end, when the kingdom goes over to his son, Murcia will still be his. The palace he walks into has since disappeared under convent and cathedral. The precinct is known; the rooms are not.
suggested_refs: The Alcazar Mayor of Murcia, absorbed into the later cathedral and convent precinct

stops.name: Campo de Mirra, the Treaty of Almizra
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: 26 March 1244. The coordinate is Campo de Mirra per es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campo_de_Mirra; an earlier pool coordinate pointed at Villena, some kilometres off. Jaime I signed in person.
stops.campa: At Almizra, in the hills behind Villena, Jaime I of Aragon and the Castilian heir draw a line across land neither crown yet holds. North and east of it is to be Aragon's to conquer, south and west Castile's. Jaime signs in person. Five years on Alfonso will marry his daughter and the line will be held by a bed as well as by a seal, and twenty-two years on Jaime will cross it with an army to do Castile a favour. The village is called Campo de Mirra now.
suggested_refs: The Treaty of Almizra, 26 March 1244, partition of the unconquered south between Castile and Aragon

stops.name: Jaen, in his father's host
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction [R]: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_de_Castilla establishes his presence in the expansionary army but not an independent command. Month and day not fixed.
stops.campa: Fernando III brings the army up under the hill of Santa Catalina and Jaen comes over, and with it the submission of Granada, which agrees to tribute and to sending troops to Castilian sieges. Within two years the Nasrid king will be sending those men down the open road to the siege of Seville. Alfonso is twenty-four and is in the host. What he did in it no source reached here says, and the royal historiography written later says a good deal more than the record supports.
suggested_refs: The Castillo de Santa Catalina above Jaen and the 1246 Nasrid submission to tributary status

stops.name: Seville, the city falls and the minaret stands
stops.date_confidence: attested for the fall of Seville in 1248 and for Alfonso's presence among the besieging princes; the day of the formal entry is given variously and is used here only to order the segment.
stops.campa: After months of siege and a broken bridge of boats, Seville surrenders. Fernando III enters with his sons in December and the Almohad congregational mosque becomes a cathedral with its minaret left standing. Alfonso is twenty-six. He will spend more of his life in this city than in any other: he will be proclaimed king in it, will write and have written in it, will be shut up in it by his own son's party, will die in it and be buried in it twice. The tower he rides past is the Giralda.
suggested_refs: The Giralda, minaret of the Almohad mosque, left standing when the mosque became the cathedral

stops.name: Valladolid, the marriage to Violante of Aragon
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_de_Castilla, boda con Violante de Aragon en la Colegiata de Valladolid, 29 January 1249.
stops.campa: He marries Violante, daughter of Jaime I, in the Colegiata of Valladolid. She is a child; he is twenty-seven. The marriage closes the line drawn at Almizra five years before and will produce ten children, among them Fernando de la Cerda and Sancho, the two sons whose rival claims will tear the last decade of the reign to pieces. In 1278 Violante will leave her husband and carry the Cerda grandsons to her brother's court in Aragon, where Sancho cannot reach them.
stops.quote: Boda con Violante de Aragón en la Colegiata de Valladolid
suggested_refs: The Colegiata of Valladolid, now the cathedral, site of the 1249 wedding

segments.name: The Crown and the Southern Frontier

stops.name: Seville, proclaimed king of Castile and Leon
stops.date_confidence: proclamation on 1 June 1252 attested. The sources contradict each other on the father's death: Cervantes Virtual gives 30 May 1252, es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_de_Castilla gives 31 May. The contradiction is left standing. The alcazar is the landmark used; the exact proclamation site is unspecified.
stops.campa: Fernando III dies in Seville and on the first of June Alfonso is proclaimed king of Castile and Leon. The sources cannot agree which day his father died, the thirtieth of May or the thirty-first; the proclamation itself is firm. He is thirty. He inherits a kingdom that has roughly doubled inside his own lifetime and a frontier that now runs along the sea. The astronomers he will employ will set the epoch of their tables at this date, so that every planetary position they compute counts forward from the day the crown changed heads.
suggested_refs: The epoch of the Alfonsine Tables, fixed at the coronation of 1 June 1252
sources: Cervantes Virtual, cronologia de Alfonso X

stops.name: The Algarve, the first campaign as king
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year by en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_of_Castile. Month, route, terms and duration of the occupation are not in the sources reached here; the coordinate is the region, not a battle site.
stops.campa: In his first full year as king he goes into Portugal and takes the Algarve. It is the kind of campaign a new king makes in order to be seen making one, against a Christian neighbour rather than a Muslim one, over a coastal strip both crowns claim and neither has settled. That he went and that he took it is attested for 1253. The route, the terms and the length of the occupation are in no source reached here. Whether he ever meant to keep the place is a question the record leaves open.
suggested_refs: The Castilian-Portuguese dispute over the Algarve and its settlement in the following years

stops.name: Jerez de la Frontera, the conquest with four dates
stops.date_confidence: contested and deliberately unresolved. es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_de_Castilla records an action in 1253 and a forced submission in late 1260 or early 1261; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerez_de_la_Frontera gives the definitive incorporation as 1264, after the Mudejar revolt, and notes recent research arguing 1266 from a royal charter. The 1253 date is the weakest of the four and is used here only to place the stop first in the sequence.
stops.campa: Castile takes Jerez, or forces its submission, or does both more than once. One article records an action in 1253 and a forced submission in the winter of 1260 to 1261. The article on the town itself says the city and its kingdom were definitively joined to the crown in 1264, after the Mudejar revolt, and adds that recent research argues for 1266 on the strength of a royal charter. Four dates circulate for one event, and the alcazar is the same building in every one of them. No source reached here reconciles them, and none of the four has been shown wrong.
suggested_refs: The Alcazar of Jerez and the documentary problem of the town's definitive incorporation

stops.name: Burgos, his sister married to the heir of England
stops.date_confidence: attested for Burgos and 1254 by en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_of_Castile; the month is an ordering device and the church is not fixed in the sources reached here.
stops.campa: His sister Leonor is married at Burgos to the son of Henry III of England, the Edward who will be Edward I. The treaty behind the marriage buys off an English claim on Gascony and gives Castile a friend in the north. Alfonso is twenty-two months into his reign and is already working the map by marriage rather than by siege. The sources fix the city and the year; they do not fix the church. Somewhere in that same town his mother has been in the ground at Las Huelgas for nineteen years.
suggested_refs: The Anglo-Castilian treaty of 1254 and the Gascon claim it settled

stops.name: Seville, the heir and the second son
stops.date_confidence: births attested for 1255 (Fernando de la Cerda) and 1258 (Sancho) by en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_of_Castile; the place is given only as Castile, and Seville here is a placement for the itinerant court, not an attestation.
stops.campa: Violante bears him Fernando, called de la Cerda, the eldest son and the intended heir. Three years later comes Sancho. Between the two boys there is nothing visible: an heir and a spare, a normal arrangement. Everything in the last ten years of the reign comes out of the gap between them, out of a father who keeps faith with a dead son's children and a second son who holds that a kingdom under attack belongs to whoever can defend it. None of that exists in 1255. The place of both births is given in the sources only as Castile.
suggested_refs: The Cerda claim and the Castilian succession dispute of 1275-1304

stops.name: Sale, the raid across the strait
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1260 by es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_de_Castilla; month and day are not fixed and Alfonso's personal presence with the fleet is not established there.
stops.campa: A Castilian fleet crosses to the Moroccan coast and sacks Sale at the mouth of the Bou Regreg. It is a raid and not a conquest: the ships come, the port burns, the ships leave. Whether Alfonso sailed with them is not established in any source reached here. He has been king eight years and is already thinking past the strait, toward the African campaign his grandfather's generation would have called the completion of the work. The Marinids on that shore remember it. Eighteen years later it will be their fleet doing the surprising, and his ships burning off Algeciras.
suggested_refs: The 1260 sack of Sale and the Castilian design on North Africa

stops.name: Niebla, the last taifa of the southwest
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_de_Castilla, Niebla fue conquistada a continuacion, en febrero de 1262. The day is not given.
stops.campa: Niebla, the last Muslim polity in the southwest still running its own affairs, falls in February after a siege long enough to be remembered. With it the map of al-Andalus reduces to Granada, which pays tribute and sends soldiers, and to a scatter of Mudejar towns under Castilian lords. Alfonso is forty, and in the south he has finished what his father began. The next war on this frontier will come not from a taifa but from the Muslims already living inside his kingdom. Of the fall itself the chronicle keeps two words: con facilidad, easily.
stops.quote: Niebla fue conquistada a continuación, en febrero de 1262, con facilidad.
suggested_refs: The Castillo de Niebla and the end of the southwestern taifas

stops.name: Cadiz, the port built for a crossing
stops.date_confidence: contested year. The chronology of the reign puts the repopulation at 1262; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadiz says the city was incorporated into the Crown of Castile in 1264, having belonged to the Marinid sultanate. Both are recorded and neither is preferred here.
stops.campa: He sets about repopulating Cadiz on its spit of rock and loads it with everything a town can be given: tax privileges, the status of a city, a bishop's seat, a monopoly on trade with Africa. It is meant to be the harbour an army crosses from. The army never crosses and the harbour is built anyway. The reign's chronology dates the work to 1262; the city's own account says it passed from the Marinid sultanate to Castile in 1264, and that the king gave it its tax privileges, its city status and its bishop. Two years apart, and the sources reached here do not reconcile them.
suggested_refs: The Alfonsine repopulation of Cadiz and its African trade monopoly

stops.name: Jerez de la Frontera, the Mudejar revolt
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1264 by es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_de_Castilla, which lists the rising as revuelta mudejar at Jerez, Arcos, Lorca and Murcia. The month is not given.
stops.campa: The Muslims of Andalusia and Murcia rise: Jerez, Arcos, Lorca, Murcia, and behind them Muhammad I of Granada, the tributary. What is being repudiated is exactly the settlement Alfonso himself negotiated at Alcaraz twenty-one years earlier, the one that let a conquered population keep its law and its worship. Castile spends roughly two years putting it down. When it is down the terms do not come back. The Mudejar south is resettled from the north, town by town, and ceases to exist as a political body.
suggested_refs: The Mudejar revolt of 1264-1266 and the repopulation of Andalusia and Murcia that followed

stops.name: Murcia, restored by his father-in-law's army
stops.date_confidence: attested for January 1266 in the standard account; the day is not given, and the month comes from the atlas dossier rather than from a primary source re-fetched in this pass.
stops.campa: Jaime I of Aragon, who drew the line at Almizra twenty-two years ago and whose daughter is queen of Castile, brings his army into rebel Murcia in January, takes the city, and hands it straight back. It is the one occasion in the reign when a foreign king repairs Castile on Castile's behalf. The city that came to Alfonso by negotiation in 1243 returns to him by somebody else's siege. The Aragonese go home. The Castilian resettlement of Murcia begins the same year.
suggested_refs: Jaime I of Aragon's Murcian campaign of 1265-1266, undertaken for his son-in-law

stops.name: Salamanca, the Estudio General endowed
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1254 by Cervantes Virtual's chronology and es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_de_Castilla. The same chronology records creation of an Estudio General at Seville under the same year; whether those are two foundations or one policy applied twice is not resolved here.
stops.campa: He gives the Estudio General of Salamanca privileges and fixed salaries, chair by chair, in a royal charter: masters paid out of the crown's revenue, books guaranteed, the school made a thing of the king rather than of the bishop. The same chronology records the creation of an Estudio General at Seville under the same year, and whether those are two foundations or one policy applied twice it does not settle. A kingdom that has just doubled in size needs men who can write inside it. The charter is dated 1254.
suggested_refs: The Escuelas Mayores of Salamanca and the Alfonsine charters of privilege
sources: Cervantes Virtual, cronologia de Alfonso X

stops.name: Seville, the Fuero Real and the Especulo
stops.date_confidence: contested: Cervantes Virtual dates the completion of the Fuero Real to 1254, es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_de_Castilla to 1255, and both are left standing. The Especulo is given as 1255. The place is a placement only: neither source localizes the drafting, and the court was itinerant.
stops.campa: A royal law code is finished and begins to be granted, town by town, to stand in place of the local fuero each place has carried since its own reconquest. One chronology dates the Fuero Real to 1254 and another to 1255, and the two are left here as they stand. Alongside it a second compilation, the Especulo, dated 1255, which may be a first draft of something far larger. Where either text was written down nobody records. The court has no building; it has a baggage train.
suggested_refs: The Fuero Real and its grant to Castilian towns in place of local fueros
sources: Cervantes Virtual, cronologia de Alfonso X

stops.name: Seville, the Libro de las Leyes begun
stops.date_confidence: attested: the prologue of the work frames composition between 1256 and 1265, per es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_de_Castilla. The place is a placement for the itinerant court and is not attested.
stops.campa: Work begins on the compilation that will be called the Siete Partidas: seven books running from God down to the punishment of crime, written in Castilian for a kingdom that has been governing in Latin and in local custom. Its own prologue dates the composition from 1256 to 1265, and revision will go on after that. The first law of the first title does not open on jurisdiction, nor on the king, nor on the realm. It opens on the man who makes laws and on what he is required to love.
stops.quote: The law-maker should love God and keep Him before his eyes when he makes the laws
stops.quote_source: Siete Partidas, Part I, Title I, Law XI, Samuel Parsons Scott translation, as quoted in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siete_Partidas
suggested_refs: Samuel Parsons Scott's 1931 English translation of the Siete Partidas, re-edited by Robert I. Burns (University of Pennsylvania Press, 2001)

stops.name: Seville, the Partidas closed
stops.date_confidence: attested as the terminal date given in the work's own prologue; the code was not promulgated in Alfonso's lifetime. Place is a placement for the itinerant court.
stops.campa: Nine years of drafting close on a code his own reign never puts into force. It defines a people as the union of all men together, those of superior, middle and inferior rank. It requires of a knight prudence, fortitude, temperance and justice, and the practical knowledge to judge a horse and a weapon. It says no one escapes the penalties of the laws by saying he did not know of them. And it defines the tyrant, seven years before his nobles renounce him and seventeen before he passes judicial sentence on his own son.
stops.quote: A tyrant means a lord who has obtained possession of some kingdom, or country, by force, fraud, or treason
stops.quote_source: Siete Partidas, Part II, Title I, Law X, Samuel Parsons Scott translation, as quoted in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siete_Partidas
suggested_refs: Siete Partidas II.x.1 on the people, II.xxi.4 on the four virtues of a knight, I.i.20 on ignorance of the law
The printed editions: Alonso Diaz de Montalvo, Seville 1491; Gregorio Lopez, Salamanca 1555; Real Academia de la Historia, 1807, declared official 1818

segments.name: The Workshops of Toledo and Seville

stops.name: Toledo, the Ghaya ordered into Castilian
stops.date_confidence: attested for the window 1256-1258 by the prologue of the Latin version, per en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picatrix. The precise year inside the window and the translator's name are not recorded, and no source names the city; Toledo is the canonical placement used across the atlas for this commission.
stops.campa: He orders the Ghayat al-Hakim, the Aim of the Sage, turned out of Arabic into Castilian. The Latin prologue of the version made from it dates the work between 1256 and 1258. It travels under the name of Maslama al-Majriti, the Cordoban astronomer, an attribution modern scholarship no longer accepts, and no source reached here names the translator or the city he worked in. At this court the book is filed with the astronomy, because at this court it is astronomy. It is a manual of astral magic: how to pull a planet's power down into a figure, what to carve, what to burn, at which hour.
suggested_refs: David Pingree, Picatrix: The Latin Version of the Ghayat al-hakim (Warburg Institute, 1986)
Dan Attrell and David Porreca, Picatrix: A Medieval Treatise on Astral Magic (Penn State University Press, 2019)
sources: Gap stated: no source consulted names the city of the Castilian translation

stops.name: Seville, the court that will not sit still
stops.date_confidence: not established as a dated event: the stop records the itinerancy of the scriptorium, which no source localizes year by year. 1257 orders the segment and nothing more.
stops.campa: The scriptorium has no building. It travels with the king between Toledo, Seville and Murcia, notaries and astronomers and Jewish, Muslim and Christian translators moving with their boxes, so that a book begun in one alcazar is finished in another. Which of the cities saw the Castilian Ghaya written down is recorded nowhere. The Real Alcazar here, rebuilt in the Andalusi manner by Christian kings who kept the craftsmen on, is as plausible a room for it as anything standing in Toledo.
suggested_refs: The Real Alcazar of Seville under Alfonso X, one working residence of the itinerant court
sources: Gap stated explicitly: the itinerary of the scriptorium is not documented city by city

stops.name: Segovia, the hall comes down on the king
stops.date_confidence: the collapse is attested [A]: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazar_de_Segovia, en 1258, reinando Alfonso X, se hundio el palacio cuando el rey se encontraba en su interior. The blasphemy legend attached to it is [R] and is not in that article at all. No fire at Segovia under Alfonso is recorded; the building's documented fires are 1681 and 1862.
stops.campa: Part of the palace of the Alcazar of Segovia falls in while the king is inside it. He is not hurt. The Spanish record of the building says only that: the palace collapsed, with Alfonso in it. There is no fire in the account and no storm. After his death the collapse is retold as a judgement, a roof brought down on a king who had said that if God had taken his advice at the creation he would have recommended something simpler. No document of his own reign contains the remark.
stops.quote: If the Lord Almighty had consulted me before embarking on creation thus, I should have recommended something simpler.
stops.quote_source: Posthumous legend, wording as circulated via Owen Gingerich (1990), quoted in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_of_Castile; apocryphal, rejected as early as Jeronimo de Zurita in the sixteenth century
suggested_refs: The Alcazar of Segovia and the 1258 structural collapse behind the blasphemy legend

stops.name: Toledo, the Libro de las cruces and the men who made it
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction [R]: Cervantes Virtual's chronology places the astrological and astronomical translation work at Toledo across roughly 1259-1272. The single year is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Jewish and Christian specialists work at Toledo under royal commission on the astrological corpus, translating out of Arabic and revising the Castilian, and among what they produce is the Libro de las cruces, a book of judgements on the crossings of the planets. The king's part is editorial and the prologues say so: he had it corrected, he had the Castilian made plain. Two names carry most of the weight, Yehuda ben Moshe ha-Cohen and Isaac ben Sid, called Rabicag, and of either man's life almost nothing is recorded.
suggested_refs: The Libro de las cruces and the Alfonsine astrological corpus
Yehuda ben Moshe ha-Cohen and Isaac ben Sid (Rabicag), the court's principal named collaborators, neither of whom has a journey of his own
sources: Cervantes Virtual, cronologia de Alfonso X

stops.name: Toledo, the observations begin
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction [R]: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_of_Castile gives roughly a decade of observation beginning around 1262. The start year is not firm and no month is recorded.
stops.campa: Astronomers begin a decade of observation at Toledo, meant to correct the planetary tables Latin Europe has been working from. What comes out is called the Alfonsine Tables, and it counts from the first of June 1252: the epoch of the tables is the day he was crowned. The Castilian text does not survive. What survives is a Latin revision made at Paris in the following century, and that is the version that becomes the working instrument of European astronomy, printed in 1483 and again in 1492 and not displaced until 1627.
suggested_refs: The Latin Alfonsine Tables, first printed 1483, second edition 1492, superseded by Kepler's Rudolphine Tables in 1627
Nicolaus Copernicus owned and had bound a printed copy of the Alfonsine Tables while a student at Krakow; that is his engagement, on his own journey, not Alfonso's

stops.name: Seville, the first book of the Cantigas
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1274 as the date of the first compilation by es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_de_Castilla; the place is a placement for the itinerant court. The manuscript codices at El Escorial and Florence are produced in the early 1280s, up to his death.
stops.campa: The first compilation of the Cantigas de Santa Maria is made: hundreds of songs to the Virgin, in Galician-Portuguese rather than in the Castilian prose he has spent twenty years building, with their melodies notated and their miracles painted beside them. The prologue speaks in the first person about why a man troubles to make verse at all. How much of the cycle is his own hand is argued still: Mettmann gave many of the songs to Airas Nunes, and the question has not been closed.
stops.quote: Porque trovar es cosa en que yace / entendimiento, por ende quien lo hace / ha de tenerlo y razón suficiente / para que entienda y sepa cantar / lo que entiende y le place expresar;
stops.quote_source: Cantigas de Santa Maria, prologue, modernized Castilian rendering quoted in es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantigas_de_Santa_Maria, section Autoria; not the Galician-Portuguese original and not the Kulp-Hill English translation
suggested_refs: The four codices: the Toledo codex (BNE), the Codice Rico and the Musicians' Codex at El Escorial, and the unfinished Florence codex with its empty staves
Cantiga 100, Santa Maria, strela do dia

stops.name: Soria, the embassy from Pisa
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1256 and for Soria: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_de_Castilla. Month and day are not given. The April 1257 election took place in Germany and Alfonso was not present at it.
stops.campa: An embassy from the republic of Pisa reaches him at Soria and offers to back his candidacy for the German crown. His mother was a Hohenstaufen, the throne is vacant since the death of William of Holland, and the Pisans want a patron. He agrees. In April of the next year a divided electoral body in Germany chooses him and Richard of Cornwall both, without either of them there. The Castilian chronicles have a name for what follows, the fecho del Imperio, the business of the Empire. It begins at Soria in 1256 and runs nineteen years.
stops.quote: En 1256 Alfonso X recibía una embajada de la república de Pisa en Soria.
suggested_refs: The double imperial election of April 1257 and the long Castilian candidacy

stops.name: Beaucaire, the interview with Gregory X
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1275 and for Beaucaire by es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_de_Castilla; the month is an ordering device, the meeting ran over part of the year.
stops.campa: He crosses into Provence to put his imperial claim in front of the one man who can confirm it, and meets Gregory X on the Rhone at Beaucaire. Rudolf of Habsburg has already been elected and the pope has already decided. Alfonso argues, is refused, and gives up the pursuit. Nineteen years, two elections, embassies, subsidies, and a sum of money the kingdom will be paying for after his death, and he has never once set foot in Germany. He turns for home.
stops.quote: 1275, Beaucaire: Entrevista con papa Gregorio X donde renuncia aspiraciones imperiales
suggested_refs: The Chateau de Beaucaire on the Rhone, site of the 1275 interview

stops.name: Beaucaire, word that the heir is dead
stops.date_confidence: the death of Fernando de la Cerda at Villa Real in 1275 is attested (O'Callaghan, The Learned King, 1993; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_de_Castilla). Where the news reached Alfonso is not recorded; the stop is pinned at Beaucaire, where he is known to have been that year, and the month orders the sequence. The death itself is his son's stop, not his.
stops.campa: Fernando de la Cerda, twenty years old, dies at Villa Real while mustering an army against a Marinid invasion. His father is in Provence, hundreds of miles away, arguing about an empire he will never enter. The heir is dead and the heir's sons are small children. Sancho, the second son, takes the field, throws the invasion back, and will argue from that day forward that a kingdom under attack passes to the man who can hold it. Where the news reached the king the sources do not say.
suggested_refs: Joseph F. O'Callaghan, The Learned King: The Reign of Alfonso X of Castile (1993), on the succession crisis of 1275

segments.name: The King Against His Own House

stops.name: Burgos, the nobles renounce their homage
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1272 by es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_de_Castilla, which gives only Castile as the place. Burgos is a placement for the Castilian court and head city, not an attestation; month and day are not recorded.
stops.campa: Nuno Gonzalez de Lara, Lope Diaz III de Haro and the king's own brother the infante Felipe take the great nobility out of their homage, over taxation and over the new law, the code that sets out what a lord owes. They ride with their men into Granada, to the Nasrid king who is Castile's tributary, and bargain against their own sovereign from there. The revolt is settled in 1273 by concession. Alfonso buys back the men who left him. The Spanish account gives only Castile as the place and gives no month.
suggested_refs: The noble revolt of 1272-1273 and the Castilian magnates' exile in Granada

stops.name: Burgos, the privilege to the shepherds
stops.date_confidence: split tags. 1273 is attested [A] for the royal privilege: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesta describes the Concejo de la Mesta as creado en el Reino de Castilla en 1273. The founding of the institution is [R]: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_de_Castilla says the exact year is unknown and must fall between 1230 and 1263. Place is a placement.
stops.campa: He grants privileges to the Honrado Concejo de la Mesta, the association of the migrating flocks, and fixes in law the right of the great sheep herds to their drove roads across the kingdom, north in summer, south in winter, through anybody's fields. The Spanish account of the Mesta dates its creation to this grant. The account of his own reign says the year of the founding is unknown and must lie somewhere between 1230 and 1263, which would make 1273 the year the crown put its seal on something already running.
suggested_refs: The Honrado Concejo de la Mesta and the canadas reales

stops.name: Burgos, the killing of the infante Fadrique
stops.date_confidence: contested and unresolved. es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_de_Castilla places the conspiracy in 1277 and says the king ordered the chief plotters executed after recovering from illness, without dating the executions; Cervantes Virtual's chronology reads 1278: conjuracion y muerte del infante don Fadrique. An earlier pool note wrongly claimed Cervantes Virtual supported 1277. Place is a placement: the sources give only Castile.
stops.campa: He has his brother, the infante Fadrique, put to death, and with him Simon Ruiz de los Cameros. No formal charge survives. One account places a conspiracy in 1277 and says only that the king, recovering from an illness, ordered the principal plotters executed; another chronology puts the conspiracy and Fadrique's death under 1278. What the record establishes is the killing and not its warrant. The man who wrote the definition of a tyrant kills his own brother on no trial that anyone wrote down.
suggested_refs: The conspiracy of 1277 and the executions of the infante Fadrique and Simon Ruiz de los Cameros
sources: Cervantes Virtual, cronologia de Alfonso X

stops.name: Seville, the sentence against Sancho
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction [R] as to the exact day: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_de_Castilla carries 9 November 1282 for the testamentary disinheriting, corroborated only by the atlas dossier. The Valladolid assembly of 21 April 1282 that stripped him of government is attested [A], but it was summoned by Sancho and is Sancho's scene, not his father's.
stops.campa: In April his son summoned an assembly at Valladolid that took the government out of his hands, and most of the kingdom went with the son. By November he holds Seville, a few loyal towns, and little else. From the alcazar he issues a judicial sentence and testamentary provisions disinheriting Sancho, naming the Cerda grandsons in his place, and cursing him. He is sixty years old, he has been king thirty years, and the instrument he reaches for is a document. The date on it is 9 November 1282.
suggested_refs: The Valladolid assembly of 21 April 1282 and the testamentary disinheriting of November 1282

stops.name: Seville, asking the Marinids for an army
stops.date_confidence: the alliance with Abu Yusuf Yaqub is a documented political reversal of 1282-1283; the month here orders the sequence. The detail that Alfonso pledged or deposited his crown as security is [R] and could not be traced to any primary document in this pass. It is carried as reported tradition only.
stops.campa: Shut into Seville, he asks for troops from Abu Yusuf Yaqub, the Marinid sultan whose coast his ships raided at Sale and whose invasion his dead heir rode out to meet, and he gets them. He fights his son with the army of the power he spent a reign preparing to cross the strait against. The reversal itself is documented. The detail everyone repeats, that he pledged or deposited his crown with the sultan as security for the loan, is not: no primary source for it was traced in this pass.
suggested_refs: The Castilian-Marinid alliance of 1282-1283 and the tradition of the pledged crown
sources: Unconfirmed: the crown-as-collateral detail could not be traced to a primary document in this pass

stops.name: Seville, the Libro de los juegos finished
stops.date_confidence: attested by the colophon of the Escorial manuscript, which states that the book was begun and completed in Seville in 1283: Real Biblioteca del Monasterio de El Escorial, MS T-I-6, catalogue item 13125.
stops.campa: The last of the great books is finished in this city by his command: the Libro de los juegos, chess and dice and tables, problems set out with their boards painted beside them, and the players drawn as Muslim and Christian and Jewish, men and women, kings and nuns, sitting on the same cushions over the same board. The colophon says it was begun and completed in Seville in 1283. He has a year to live, the kingdom is at war with itself, and the workshop is painting two women at chess.
suggested_refs: Real Biblioteca del Monasterio de El Escorial, MS T-I-6, the Libro de los juegos de ajedrez, dados y tablas
sources: Real Biblioteca del Monasterio de El Escorial catalogue, item 13125

segments.name: The Body and Its Three Graves

stops.name: Seville, the death in the alcazar city
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_de_Castilla and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X_of_Castile. The immediate cause of death is not recorded.
stops.campa: Alfonso dies in Seville on the fourth of April, about sixty-two years old. The cause is not recorded anywhere. Sancho has held the government for two years; the disinheriting sentence of 1282 is a sheet of parchment that will give the Cerda line a claim and give Castile a succession war to fight over it for a generation. He was proclaimed king in this city, buried his father in it, and wrote or had written in it the greater part of everything he leaves. His will asks for the body here and the heart elsewhere.
suggested_refs: The Castilian succession war between the Cerda line and Sancho IV

stops.name: Seville Cathedral, the first burial
stops.date_confidence: attested that he was buried in Seville Cathedral beside his parents. The Capilla Real now shown as his burial place did not exist in 1284: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilla_Real_de_la_Catedral_de_Sevilla dates its construction from 1551. The April day is an ordering device.
stops.campa: He is buried in the cathedral of Seville beside Fernando III and beside Beatriz of Suabia, whose bones he had brought down from Burgos five years earlier so that the three of them would lie together. The chapel visitors are shown today as his grave is not the chapel he was put into. That building does not exist yet and will not for two hundred and sixty-seven years; it is begun in 1551, under Martin de Gainza, and stands finished and empty of kings for four years before anyone is carried into it. In 1284 he goes into the old royal chapel of the converted mosque, the one his father's generation made out of the Almohad building.
stops.quote: Sepultura: Capilla Real de la Catedral de Sevilla
suggested_refs: The old royal chapel of the converted Almohad mosque, demolished in the rebuilding of Seville Cathedral

stops.name: Murcia Cathedral, the heart sent to the loyal city
stops.date_confidence: the deposit of heart and entrails at Murcia in 1284 is attested; the month is an ordering device. The transfer into the cathedral's main chapel in 1525, at the request of the Murcian council and by order of Charles V, is attested by es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catedral_de_Murcia. A municipal press release at web.murcia.es prints 1425, which is impossible and is a typo in that source. The forensic detail of the incisions is [R].
stops.campa: His heart and entrails are cut out and sent to Murcia, the city he took by negotiation at twenty-one, lost to revolt at forty-two, and had handed back to him by his father-in-law's army, and which stayed with him when the kingdom went to his son. Tradition gives the loyalty as the reason; the will gives no reason. They go first to Santa Maria la Real and then, in 1525, by order of Charles V, into a stone urn in the cathedral's main chapel. A later examination found two careful parallel cuts in the left ribcage.
suggested_refs: The urn of Alfonso X in the Capilla Mayor of Murcia Cathedral; restorations of 1854, after a fire, and 1997, for capillary humidity; agreement of 11 August 2025 between the Murcian council and the Diocese of Cartagena for a further restoration
sources: web.murcia.es, Murcia recupera el sepulcro de Alfonso X el Sabio en la catedral
museodelaciudad.murcia.es, on the burial goods and the forensic examination

stops.name: Seville, moved into the chapel built for him
stops.date_confidence: attested: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilla_Real_de_la_Catedral_de_Sevilla states that the remains of the monarchs buried in Seville Cathedral were not moved into the new Capilla Real until 1579, under Felipe II. Construction began 1551 under Martin de Gainza and most work was finished by 1575. No month given.
stops.campa: Two hundred and ninety-five years after the funeral, Philip II has the kings moved: Fernando III, Beatriz of Suabia, Alfonso X, carried out of the old chapel and into the new Capilla Real, where they lie now. The chapel was begun in 1551 under Martin de Gainza and largely finished by 1575, and stood four years waiting. Nothing about the move is hidden; it is written down in the chapel's own construction record. It is simply forgotten by nearly everyone who stands in front of the urn and reads the date 1284 on it. The transfer is dated 1579.
suggested_refs: The Capilla Real of Seville Cathedral, begun 1551 by Martin de Gainza, occupied by the royal dead in 1579

stops.name: Seville, the tomb opened at the seventh centenary
stops.date_confidence: attested: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilla_Real_de_la_Catedral_de_Sevilla records new sepulchres built in 1948 for Alfonso X and Beatriz de Suabia for the seventh centenary of the Christian conquest of Seville, with the tomb opened during the work. The inventory of the burial goods is [R], from museodelaciudad.murcia.es. No month given.
stops.campa: For the seventh centenary of the taking of Seville new sepulchres are built in the royal chapel for Alfonso and for his mother, and in the building of them the tomb is opened. What is inside gets written down: tunics worked in gold with castles and lions, a linen cap bordered with pearls and coral, gloves, a silk purse, three pillows, three rings for the three theological virtues, and at the feet the skeleton of a small dog. The crown, the sword, the sceptre and the baton that earlier records list are already gone.
suggested_refs: The 1948 opening of the Seville tomb and the inventory of the ajuar
sources: museodelaciudad.murcia.es, Alfonso X se hizo enterrar con un rico ajuar lleno de simbolismo
